explanations.explanation: Isaiah says the Lord is seated on a throne, high and exalted, and the train of His robe fills the temple. The whole temple, baker. I can barely get my apron on without knocking over a cooling rack. Isaiah tells it as plainly as he saw it.

Bright light is a fair guess, but Isaiah doesn't say it. What fills the temple in verse 1 is the train of His robe. Something else fills the temple later, and that something is smoke (Isaiah 6:4). So it's a different verse and a different answer.
A river in the temple would make for a very squishy morning, friend. Isaiah never mentions one. He sees the Lord on a high, exalted throne, and the train of His robe fills the temple.

I can see why you'd say it, since the seraphim are flying. But Isaiah says each one has six wings and uses them three ways. With two they cover their faces, with two they cover their feet, and with two they are flying. That's only a third of the wings doing the flying.

That's right. Each seraph has six wings, and Isaiah says that with two they cover their faces, with two they cover their feet, and with two they are flying. So only two of the six are doing the flying. The other four are busy covering.

That's it. The seraphim call out, “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Hosts; all the earth is full of His glory.” They're calling to one another, and holy is the word they keep saying. I think when creatures with six wings repeat a word, it's worth remembering.
Nothing in their call says far away. The seraphim say that all the earth is full of His glory. They call Him “holy” three times in a row, and that's the heart of what they say.
That one isn't in their call, friend. The seraphim don't say anything about timing here. They call out, “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Hosts…” and then say that all the earth is full of His glory.

You'd think a doorpost would hold its ground, but these ones don't. Isaiah says that at the sound of the seraphim's voices, the doorposts and thresholds shook. So the statement that they stay perfectly still isn't what the text says. Voices alone did that.

Right, they don't stay still. Isaiah says that at the sound of their voices the doorposts and thresholds shook. That's doorposts and thresholds shaking from voices alone. I've never had a doorpost shake at anything I've said, and I've said some LOUD things.

Yes, the temple was filled with smoke. Isaiah says it happens at the sound of their voices, while the doorposts and thresholds are shaking. He doesn't say where the smoke came from, so I won't either. I'll just say it sounds like a day I would not want to be in a bakery.
Light is a natural guess with all that glory around. But Isaiah says the temple was filled with smoke. That's the word he uses in verse 4.

The seraphim are calling out, so it makes sense to think music. But Isaiah doesn't call it that, and he says the temple was filled with smoke. The voices come with the doorposts and thresholds shaking, and the temple filled with smoke.

explanations.answer: He is a man of unclean lips
explanations.explanation: That's what Isaiah says. “Woe is me, for I am ruined, because I am a man of unclean lips…” He says it because his eyes have seen the King, the LORD of Hosts. I think seeing the King made him look at himself honestly.

explanations.answer: He is a man of slow speech
explanations.explanation: That sounds like Moses, Israel's leader, who told the Lord he was slow of speech (Exodus 4:10). Isaiah says something different. He calls himself a man of unclean lips. Two different men in two different moments, friend.

explanations.answer: He is the least in his father's house
explanations.explanation: That's closer to Gideon, a leader in Israel, who called himself the youngest in his father's house (Judges 6:15). Isaiah doesn't talk about his family at all here. What he says about himself is that he is a man of unclean lips.

It would be easier if it were just him, but Isaiah doesn't say that. He says he is “…a man of unclean lips dwelling among a people of unclean lips…” He includes the people around him. So he isn't saying everyone else is just fine.

That's right. Isaiah says he is “…a man of unclean lips dwelling among a people of unclean lips…” He doesn't say he's the only one, and he doesn't say his people are fine. I like that he doesn't point fingers and just says what's true.

Yes, the seraph touches his mouth. Isaiah says the seraph touched his mouth with the coal and said, “Now that this has touched your lips…” That's the same place Isaiah named when he said he was a man of unclean lips.
Isaiah's eyes did see the King, so I understand the guess. But the coal doesn't go there. The seraph touched his mouth, and said the coal had touched his lips.

Hands would be the usual place to hold a coal, friend, and that's why it's a fun guess. But Isaiah says the seraph touched his mouth with it. The seraph even says, “Now that this has touched your lips…”

That's what the seraph says. “Now that this has touched your lips, your iniquity is removed and your sin is atoned for.” Isaiah had just called himself ruined. The seraph tells him his iniquity is gone.
Renewed strength is a nice thing to hear, but the seraph doesn't say it here. What the seraph says is that Isaiah's iniquity is removed. And his sin is atoned for.

More days would be nice, but that's not what the seraph says. After the coal touches Isaiah's lips, the seraph tells him, “Now that this has touched your lips, your iniquity is removed and your sin is atoned for.” That's the message, friend, and it's about his sin, not his years.
He does. Isaiah says, “Here am I. Send me!” The Lord asks, “Whom shall I send? Who will go for Us?” and Isaiah volunteers himself. I'd have needed at least three minutes and a cookie.

explanations.answer: He asks Him to send someone else
explanations.explanation: That sounds like Moses, Israel's leader, who asked the Lord to send someone else (Exodus 4:13). Isaiah answers the other way. He says, “Here am I. Send me!”
Staying quiet would be a safe move, friend, but Isaiah doesn't take it. When he hears the Lord ask whom He should send, he answers, “Here am I. Send me!” He volunteers himself.

Yes. The message is, “Be ever hearing, but never understanding; be ever seeing, but never perceiving.” They keep hearing and keep seeing, but they never understand. It's a heavy line, and I'll leave it as heavy as the Lord says it.
Speaking is Isaiah's part here, since he's the one told to go and tell. In the message itself, the people never understand. The Lord says, “Be ever hearing, but never understanding…”
The text doesn't say anything about rest in this message. It says they are ever hearing but never understanding, and ever seeing but never perceiving. The thing they never do is understand.

That's it. The Lord says, “Otherwise they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts, and turn and be healed.” Turning and being healed is the outcome the Lord names there. I think this is a heavy part, so read it slowly.
A new king isn't what the Lord names here. He says they might understand with their hearts, “…and turn and be healed.” Turning and healing are the words in the verse.

Altars come up in this chapter, since the coal came from one, but that's not the answer here. The Lord says that otherwise they might see, hear and understand, “…and turn and be healed.” It's about turning and being healed.

That's a shorter answer than the Lord gives. He doesn't mention a next king. He says it will be until the cities lie ruined and without inhabitant, until the houses are left unoccupied and the land is desolate and ravaged.

Right, there's no word about a next king. The Lord answers, “Until the cities lie ruined and without inhabitant, until the houses are left unoccupied and the land is desolate and ravaged…” It's a long answer to a short question. I think this one hurts to read.

Yes. The Lord says, “…until the houses are left unoccupied and the land is desolate and ravaged…” The cities lie ruined and without inhabitant, and the houses are left empty too. It's a quiet, heavy picture.
Rebuilt would be a happier ending, but that's not what the Lord says here. His answer is that the houses are left unoccupied. That's the word in verse 11.
Crowded is the opposite of what the Lord says. He says the cities lie ruined and without inhabitant, and the houses are left unoccupied. Empty houses, friend.
I wish it said that, but it doesn't. The Lord says, “And though a tenth remains in the land, it will be burned again.” So the tenth that remains is burned again, not spared.

That's right. The Lord says, “And though a tenth remains in the land, it will be burned again.” A tenth remains, but it isn't spared from the burning. The stump picture later in that same verse is where something is still left (Isaiah 6:13).

That's the one. The Lord says, “As the terebinth and oak leave stumps when felled, so the holy seed will be a stump in the land.” A stump is what's left when the tree comes down. The holy seed is that stump, still in the land.

Ash makes sense after all that burning, but the Lord's picture is a different one. He says that as the terebinth and oak leave stumps when felled, so the holy seed will be a stump in the land. It's a tree picture, not an ash picture.
A whole forest is a big jump from what the Lord says. He says that as the terebinth and oak leave stumps when felled, so the holy seed will be a stump in the land. One stump, and no forest in sight.
